subject: Civil Engineering
title: Quality Control and Assurance
description: A micro-lesson that makes Quality Control and Assurance usable.

hook.text: A concrete cylinder breaks at 2,500 psi instead of the required 4,000. What happens now?

buildup.text: Quality control tests materials and workmanship during construction — catching defects early.

discovery.text: Quality assurance sets the standards and procedures — the system that ensures QC happens.

twist.text: Non-conformance reports document failures — the fix might be removal, repair, or acceptance.

climax.text: Third-party inspectors verify work independently — the owner's eyes on the contractor's work.

punchline.text: Quality isn't inspected in — it's built in. Inspection just proves it was done right.

quiz.question: What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?
options: They are the same thing with different names
QC tests specific work for compliance; QA establishes the standards and procedures
QC is done by the owner; QA is done by the contractor

details.summary: Quality control inspects and tests completed work against specifications to identify defects, while quality assurance establishes processes and procedures that prevent defects from occurring. Together they ensure that constructed facilities meet the design requirements and will perform as intended.
details.whyItMatters: Rework due to quality failures costs 5 to 15% of total project cost on average. Preventing defects through quality assurance is far cheaper than finding and fixing them after construction.
takeaways: Quality control finds defects through inspection and testing after work is done
Quality assurance prevents defects through procedures and process controls
Inspection and test plans document what will be checked and by whom

faq.question: What is a construction inspection and test plan?
faq.answer: An ITP lists every quality verification activity for each work item: what is inspected or tested, the acceptance criteria, who performs the check, when it occurs (hold point versus witness point), and what documentation is required. It ensures systematic quality verification throughout construction.

faq.question: What is the cost of poor quality in construction?
faq.answer: Studies consistently show that rework consumes 5 to 15% of total project cost. Beyond direct rework cost, poor quality causes schedule delays, disputes, warranty claims, reduced asset life, and reputation damage. Prevention through quality systems typically costs less than 1% of project value.
